# Explicit localization to a projected marginal's deepest set

Let K be a D-dimensional convex body, with uniform probability measure
mu. Let `pi:R^D->R^r` be a surjective linear map, where `1<=r<=D`,
and let nu be the exact pushforward probability measure. Put

`B=pi K`, `Delta_B=B-B`,

and let `||.||_(Delta_B)` be the norm with unit ball Delta_B. Define

\[
 \alpha=\max_{x\in B}\operatorname{depth}_{\nu}(x),\qquad
 \mathcal A=\{x:\operatorname{depth}_{\nu}(x)=\alpha\}.
                                                               \tag{1}
\]

All depths here use closed halfspaces in the projected space. The
bounded marginal density is positive on int B. Its cap masses are
continuous jointly in a unit normal and a bounded threshold, by
dominated convergence. Hence the depth is continuous; it is zero on
the boundary, positive in the interior, and attains its maximum on B.
In particular A is nonempty and compact, and is contained in int B.
The rank-sensitive theorem in
`candidate a25f203b14ed76b3` gives
`alpha>=gamma_r`, where `gamma_0=1` and
`gamma_j=(j/(j+1))^j` for j>=1. Nothing here identifies A with the
ordinary projected centroid.

## Theorem

Suppose finitely many closed halfspaces h_i in R^r cover R^r, all their
boundaries pass through c, and

`nu(h_i)<=tau<gamma_(r-1)` for every i.

Then `c in int B`, `gamma_r<=alpha<=tau`, and for **every** `c_* in A`,

\[
 \boxed{\quad
 \|c-c_*\|_{B-B}
 \le\min\left\{1,
 \frac{D^2(\tau-\alpha)}
      {\alpha(\gamma_{r-1}-\tau)}\right\}.
 \quad}                                                       \tag{2}
\]

In particular the fully explicit, dimension-dependent consequence is

\[
 \|c-c_*\|_{B-B}
 \le\min\left\{1,
 \frac{D^2(\tau-\gamma_r)}
      {\gamma_r(\gamma_{r-1}-\tau)}\right\}.
                                                               \tag{3}
\]

If tau equals alpha, the deepest set is the singleton `{c}`. If tau
equals gamma_r, both this conclusion and `alpha=gamma_r` hold.
This is localization to an actual deepest point of the marginal, not
to its centroid. Both dimensions have explicit roles: the rank r
controls the exterior-contact threshold, while ambient dimension D
controls one-dimensional section-density estimates.

## 1. Scalar estimates in the actual ambient body

Fix a nonzero linear functional ell on R^r and normalize it to have
width one on B. Then `ell composed with pi` also has width one on K.
Let p be the probability density of this scalar functional under mu.
The same two-cone proof as in
`candidate e81e0e86f9a482f3` gives

\[
                          0\le p(t)\le D.                    \tag{4}
\]

For clarity: a section of K and the two support points on either side
span two cones contained in K whose combined height is the full width.
Their total volume yields section density at most D in unit-width
coordinates. Thus threshold movement a changes a cap fraction upward
by at most `D(a)_+`.

For D>=2, the section Brunn--Minkowski inequality says that
`p^(1/(D-1))` is concave on the scalar support interval. In particular
p is unimodal. For any `c_* in A`, write `t_*=ell(c_*)`. Both scalar
tails based at t_* have probability at least alpha. We claim

\[
                           p(t_*)\ge\alpha.                  \tag{5}
\]

Choose a level where p attains its maximum, using the upper
semicontinuous section representative on its compact support. If this
mode is to the right of t_*, unimodality bounds p(s) by p(t_*) for
all s<=t_*. The left tail has mass at most p(t_*) times an interval
length at most one. If the mode is to the left, use the right tail
instead. In either case a tail of mass at least alpha is bounded above
by p(t_*), proving (5). If D=1, the density is identically one on a
unit interval, so (4) and (5) hold directly.

Let `L=t_*-min_B ell>0`. The same concave-root interpolation with the
left endpoint gives, for `0<=a<=L` and D>=2,

\[
 \begin{split}
 \nu\{t_*-a\le\ell(x)\le t_*\}
 &\ge p(t_*)\frac L D[1-(1-a/L)^D]\\
 &\ge\frac{\alpha a}{D}.
 \end{split}                                                 \tag{6}
\]

For D=1 the slab has probability a, which also proves (6).
Hyperplanes have zero nu measure, so there is no boundary correction.

The through-c_* cap has mass at least alpha. Consequently, whenever
c belongs to B and `ell(c_*-c)>=0`,

\[
 \boxed{\quad
 \nu\{x:\ell(x-c)\ge0\}
 \ge\alpha+\frac{\alpha}{D}\ell(c_*-c).
 \quad}                                                       \tag{7}
\]

The membership c in B guarantees that the slab displacement in (7)
does not exceed L. Notice that (5), not a centroid identity, justifies
this estimate at a deepest marginal point.

## 2. Rank-sensitive conditioning of the cover normals

Write the given caps as `h_i={x:ell_i(x-c)>=0}`, with every ell_i
having width one on B. The exterior-contact part of the rank-sensitive
theorem first gives c in int B. For every v on the boundary of B-B,
the point c-v is outside int B: otherwise v would lie in the open set
`c-int B`, contained in B-B, a contradiction.

Translate all the halfspaces by -v. They still cover R^r and share the
exterior-or-boundary contact c-v. By (4), every translated halfspace
has fraction at most

`tau+D max{0,max_i ell_i(v)}`.

The exterior-contact threshold for this exact marginal is
gamma_(r-1), by Section 3 of the rank-sensitive theorem. Therefore

\[
             \max_i\ell_i(v)\ge
             \frac{\gamma_{r-1}-\tau}{D}>0.
                                                               \tag{8}
\]

In particular, the normals necessarily span R^r, even if that was not
separately required in the hypotheses: (8) excludes any common kernel
direction. Equivalently their convex hull contains
`[(gamma_(r-1)-tau)/D](B-B)^circ`.

## 3. Proof of the distance bound

The original cover contains any chosen c_* in at least one cap, so
`alpha<=tau`. If c=c_*, the conclusion is immediate. Otherwise put

`q=||c_*-c||_(B-B)>0`, `v=(c_*-c)/q in boundary(B-B)`.

By (8), some i satisfies

`ell_i(c_*-c)>=q(gamma_(r-1)-tau)/D>0`.

For this original cap, (7) yields

\[
 \tau\ge\alpha+
 \frac{\alpha q(\gamma_{r-1}-\tau)}{D^2}.
\]

Rearranging gives the second bound in (2), and `q<=1` follows from
c,c_* in B. Since `alpha>=gamma_r` and
`(tau-alpha)/alpha=tau/alpha-1` decreases with alpha, (3) follows.
Every step applies to every deepest point separately. In particular
tau=alpha forces every such point to equal c.

If `tau=gamma_r+epsilon` and
`0<=epsilon<gamma_(r-1)-gamma_r`, (3) is an explicit linear modulus
near zero. No compactness-only argument, lower bound on balancing
weights, differentiability of depth, or centroid-depth assertion is
used. The result gives a necessary geometric condition on a low-budget
common-contact cover. It makes no claim that different mixed-integer
fibers have compatible contacts or that such a cover supplies the
single mixed-integer center required by OC.
